finding: §4.2.3's brief change silently breaks a shipped tp contract the spec never mentions: `review_loop.instruction`. tp emits, in every review payload, the line 'Process the regression prompt first and apply its findings before or together with the three role prompts' (spec/0.23.0.md §8.3, verified present in this spec's own round-6 emission). Today that instruction is followable because every recipient receives the whole panel including `regression`. After §4.2.3, every review-role unit's own first command is `tp review <spec> --role <id>` with its corpus id, so no unit's payload can contain the regression prompt — while the same payload still carries the instruction telling it to process that prompt first. §4.1 measures the pre-existing waste ('emitted to everyone and executed by nobody') and §4.4 claims the release converts it into a visible loss, but §4.4's visibility is test 17, a unit test; the running loop is left with an instruction that is now unfollowable by construction rather than merely ignored. The spec's Non-Goal 7 asserts 'Changing what a round asks... untouched', which this contradicts: the instruction is exactly what the round asks.
suggestion: Rule on `review_loop.instruction` under --role explicitly. Either suppress or reword it when `prompts[]` has been reduced and the regression entry is not present, or have the driver keep exactly one unit unrestricted so the instruction retains a recipient. Add the decision to §4.2 and a test to §6.3; and if the instruction is left unchanged, say so in §4.4 rather than leaving the reader to discover that a shipped payload key became self-contradictory.

finding: §6.1 fixes only the OUTCOME of test isolation ('spec/.tp-review/ and .tp/rounds/ are byte-identical before and after the suite runs') and then declares the mechanism free: 'Whether the isolation is --no-state, a temporary state directory or a copied tree is the implementer's choice'. The three are not interchangeable, and one of them disarms the release gate. Measured on the freshly built binary against this spec: 'tp review spec/0.36.0.md --round N --no-state --json' emits exactly four prompts (architect, ax-economist, implementer, tester) at N=1, N=4 and N=6, with skipped_roles EMPTY — regression is neither emitted nor skipped, it is absent from both arrays. Under that choice test 7 has no round at which 'regression is emitted' and no skipped_roles entry carrying no-baseline, so neither half is reachable; test 9's no-baseline case likewise; tests 13 and 14 — the release's only gate — run over a four-role panel that never contains the 82,160-byte entry §4.1 calls 62% of the payload, so the gate passes green without once exercising the largest thing --role selects; and test 17's 'emitted role set minus unit set equals exactly {regression}' fails outright, because that difference is empty. Under a temporary state directory or a copied tree all four are reachable. All three mechanisms satisfy §6.1's stated outcome equally well, so nothing in the spec discriminates between a harness where the gate is armed and one where it is vacuous.
suggestion: Split §6.1's condition into an outcome and a precondition. Outcome: state unchanged, as written. Precondition: the harness must reproduce recorded review state, so that (a) a round exists at which regression is emitted and (b) round 1 exists at which regression appears in skipped_roles with reason no-baseline. Then say explicitly that --no-state does not meet it, citing the measurement above, and name the temporary state directory (seeded with a recorded round) and the copied tree as the two admissible mechanisms. Independently, add to tests 13 and 14 the assertion that the panel under test contains regression, so a harness that silently drops it fails instead of passing.

finding: §6.1 offers three isolation mechanisms as the implementer's free choice — "--no-state, a temporary state directory or a copied tree" — and fixes only the outcome (spec/.tp-review/ and .tp/rounds/ byte-identical before and after). The three are not interchangeable: two of them delete the very input the panel is derived from. Whether the built-in regression role is emitted depends on a recorded baseline (engine/skipped.go: SkipNoBaseline = "the built-in regression role at round 1, which has no snapshot-round-0.md to diff against"), and --no-state disables all review-state reads and writes outright (and review.go already refuses it with --record/--status/--check). Under --no-state, or under an empty temporary state directory, every spec emits at round 1, regression is always skipped no-baseline, and test 7's emitted-regression half, test 9's four non-no-baseline reasons, tests 13/14's panel and §7's gate all run against a panel from which the release's largest and most suppression-prone entry is structurally absent. The gate reports green while measuring nothing — the exact v0.34.0 §7.1 shape §7 was written to prevent. The implementer cannot pick correctly from what the spec says, because the spec presents the choice as free.
suggestion: Replace the free choice with the property the isolation must preserve: the isolated tree must reproduce each spec's recorded round count and its snapshot-round-*.md baselines, so the round-dependence §4.1 establishes survives. State that --no-state is not an admissible mechanism for any test whose subject is the panel (7, 9, 13, 14 and §7's gate), because it removes the state that decides the panel; a copied tree that includes spec/.tp-review/ is. Keep the byte-identity assertion as the second condition, not the only one.

finding: §7 justifies choosing repository-breadth over a fixture with a factual claim about this repository that is false, and §6.3 concedes the opposite three paragraphs earlier. §7: 'The repository has specs with deactivated roles, with domain frontmatter, with empty checklists, and at rounds where regression does and does not emit — the five skip reasons of §4.2's table, occurring for real rather than by construction.' Measured against the tree this spec ships in: no file under spec/ carries YAML frontmatter of any kind, so `disabled-by-spec` (which §4.2.1 sources from the spec's `enabled: false` override) cannot occur; none of the eight corpus roles in .tp/reviewers/ + .tp/auditors/ carries a `domains` key, and spec/0.25.0.md §3.3 makes absent `domains` mean 'every domain', so `domain-mismatch` cannot occur; all eight carry a non-empty `focus` list, so `no-checklist-items` does not occur either. `no-spec-change` requires --diff-from, which the gate does not pass. That leaves `no-baseline` — one of five. §6.3 test 9 says the opposite in plain words: 'The test builds a fixture per reason rather than asserting the two the driver happens to produce today.' So the release's only gate rests on a premise the document elsewhere denies, and the sentence 'A suppression that only appears on one of those shapes passes every fixture test and fails here' is unsupported for four of the five shapes. This is the standard §4.5 sets for the rest of the document — 'cut for reasons that were measured, not argued' — applied to the one section that was not measured.
suggestion: Either (a) state the true set — the repository supplies breadth in spec size, section count, round number and regression presence, not in the five skip reasons — and drop the skip-reason claim from §7, or (b) keep the claim and make the release also add the missing shapes to the repository (a domain-carrying role file, a spec with an `enabled: false` override), so the gate's premise is created rather than asserted. Do not leave §7 and §6.3 test 9 disagreeing about what the repository contains.

finding: §1 and Non-Goal 7 both enumerate this release's surface and both omit its only change outside the emitter. §1: 'This release makes the emitted prompt self-sufficient and lets a caller ask for one role's prompt instead of the panel's.' Non-Goal 7: 'The checklist items, role rules and output schema are untouched. The prompt does gain two behavioural clauses — that is §2 and §3, and §1 prices them; the claim here is narrower than "nothing changes".' Both are emission-side only. §4.2.3 changes `UnitKind.BriefCommand` for `review-role` and `audit-role`, which changes `tp resume`'s `next_units[].brief_command` — a machine-readable output surface that the driver, the plugin agents and any external orchestrator consume, and which spec/0.35.0.md §3.3.1 fixed. §4.2.3 calls it 'the half an earlier draft omitted' and §4.5 item 1 records that omitting exactly this half is what killed --out-dir; §1.1 then reinforces the omission with '§4's flag adds no prompt bytes and removes them from what a unit receives', which is true of the prompt and silent about the brief. A reader who stops after §1 and §5 — the two sections written to be read that way — does not learn that this release modifies tp's driver contract.
suggestion: Add the brief-command change to §1's one-sentence statement of what the release does, and to Non-Goal 7's 'the claim here is narrower than nothing changes' paragraph, in the same style §1.1 uses for the prompt bytes. Both places already carry an explicit hedge; the hedge should name the change it is hedging.

finding: §1.1 is the release's cost accounting and it prices only the term this release controls least. Measured just now, round 6, current binary, TP_* cleared (the protocol §4.1 itself fixes): the payload is 172,778 B over 5 prompts and one corpus role prompt is 20,965 B. Segmenting that prompt: the UNRESOLVED-findings block is 6,883 B (33%), the verbatim changed-spec-section block is 6,744 B (32%) and the structured-element checklist is 4,181 B (20%) - 85% of every role prompt is derived history and this spec's own prose. Against §4.1's own round-4 row (131,727 B, corpus roles 12,321-12,472 B each), two repair rounds added 41,051 B of payload and grew each corpus role prompt by ~8,400 B (+68%), while the spec file went 18,647 B -> 39,510 B (+112%) and the mechanism it specifies - two fixed strings totalling 464 B and one flag - did not change size at all. So the release adds ~18x more bytes per role prompt per round through its own rationale prose than the 467 B §1.1 tabulates, and the section that exists to price the release does not name that term. This is not the round-3 denominator finding (§1.1 now gives both denominators correctly); the numerator set is what is incomplete.
suggestion: Add one row or one sentence to §1.1 stating the measured per-round prose cost alongside the 467 B, with the round it was measured on - or, if it is out of scope, fence it explicitly in §5 by naming spec/0.40.0.md (repair verbosity) as its owner. Then move the settled rejected-design narration that carries no contract - §2.4's copy-out history, §4.5's four items, §6.1's dead-end drafts, §7's third and fourth paragraphs - into spec/0.36.0-candidates.md or the repair commit messages, so a round that re-reviews this spec pays for the contract and not for the argument.

finding: §4.2.1 places a normative requirement on the UNIT — 'A unit that receives no prompt still creates its findings file, empty' — and neither routes it to the unit nor tests it. It cannot arrive through the emitted prompt: §2.3's emission predicate appends both clauses 'to every prompt whose output_path is non-empty, and to no other', and this unit's own invocation returns prompts: [], so it receives no prompt, no output_path and neither clause. It cannot arrive through the agent definitions either, since §2.4 says those are 'loaded by nothing on the interactive path'. And §6 does not assert it: of the seventeen numbered tests the only one that touches this unit is test 16, which executes the brief_command and asserts exit 0 — a 'tp review --role X' invocation exiting 0 says nothing about whether the agent afterwards creates $TP_ROUND_DIR/role-$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson.part. So the single sentence §4.2.1 identifies as what stops the exit-0 rule from 'trading one failure for another' is the one requirement in this release with no delivery channel and no assertion, and a QA engineer cannot write a pass/fail test for it from the spec as it stands.
suggestion: Either make it emitted or make it tested, and say which. Emitted: state in §2.3 that when prompts[] is empty the payload still carries the unit's output_path (top-level, since there is no prompt to hang it on) together with a one-line instruction to create that file empty, and add a §6.2 test that the empty-panel payload contains that path. Tested: add a §6.4 test that, on the same no-checklist-items fixture test 16 already requires, runs the unit's brief and then asserts spec/0.35.0.md §3.3's predicate for $TP_ROUND_DIR/role-$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson.part — the file exists and every line parses, vacuously true at zero lines. Without one of the two, the exit-0 rule is unverified at exactly the point §4.2.1 says it matters.

finding: §4.2.1 states "A unit that receives no prompt still creates its findings file, empty" and concludes "so no hook change is needed, only the instruction" — but it never names the surface that carries the instruction, and on the exit-0 path no surface exists. The unit's only channel is the emitted prompt, and this is precisely the case where prompts[] is empty; §2.2's and §3.2's clauses are appended to a prompt body (§2.3), so neither reaches a unit that got no prompt. §3.2's clause would not help even if it arrived: "write each row as you decide it" says nothing about writing a file with zero rows. I verified the hook side of the claim is correct (hooks/stop-role-incomplete.sh does pass an empty file), so the gap is entirely on the emission side: the implementer must invent a channel the spec does not authorise, or ship the wasted round-trip §4.2.1 says it is avoiding.
suggestion: Name the channel and make it assertable. The natural home is the exit-0 payload itself, which the unit does read: require that an invocation reduced to prompts: [] carries the instruction alongside the skipped_roles entry (or in review_loop.instruction), in fixed words, and add a §6.3 test that --role <skipped-role> emits that text. If the decision is instead that the agent definitions carry it, say so and move it out of §4.2.1's "only the instruction" sentence, which currently implies no work at all.

finding: §4.2.1's exit-0 rule makes 'a dropped role merging clean' reachable by design, on a hazard tp has already named and routed elsewhere. Chain: a corpus role skipped `no-checklist-items` or `no-spec-change` is still spawned as a unit (§4.2.1's table, the two bold rows); §4.2.1 has it write an empty findings file and exit 0; spec/0.35.0.md §3.3.1's `promoteRoleFindings` renames it on exit 0 to `role-<id>.ndjson`; `tp review --merge` reads it as a valid zero-row file; `--record` counts zero non-PASS rows. The round is therefore recorded as clean for that role, and the recorded artifact is byte-indistinguishable from a role that read the whole spec and found nothing. spec/0.35.0.md §8a lists 'a dropped role merging clean' as one of the five things an unattended driver amplifies; Non-Goal 3 hands convergence arithmetic to spec/0.37.0.md, but that spec cannot distinguish these two cases because the distinguishing information — the `skipped_roles` reason — is discarded at the moment §4.2.1 tells the unit to write nothing. §4.2.1 calls this 'the correct outcome for a role that had nothing to review', which is true of the unit and false of the round.
suggestion: Have the empty-prompt unit record the skip rather than nothing: either write one row carrying the `skipped_roles` reason, or have the driver record the reason in the round's own state so `--merge`/`--record` and spec/0.37.0.md's streak arithmetic can tell a skipped role from a clean one. State in §4.2.1 which of the two, and add the assertion to §6.3 test 9 — it currently asserts only exit 0 and an echoed reason on stdout, which is the surface that does not survive into the round.

finding: §4.2.1's fix for the Stop-hook refusal has no delivery channel, and the paragraph asserts one exists. It says 'A unit that receives no prompt still creates its findings file, empty... The hook already admits the empty case... so no hook change is needed, only the instruction.' But the only channel this release adds to a unit is prompt text (§2.2, §3.2), and §2.3's emission predicate binds both clauses to 'every prompt whose output_path is non-empty, and to no other'. In the exact case §4.2.1 is ruling on, `prompts` is `[]` — there is no prompt, so there is no output_path, so there is nothing to append the instruction to. The instruction is therefore specified to be delivered on the one path where the document's own emission rule guarantees no text is delivered. §4.2.1 also does not say who else could carry it: not the agent definitions (§2.4 says they are the wrong home for the interactive path and this release does not touch them), not the hook (§4.2.1 rules that out itself), and not the brief (§4.2.3 fixes it as the bare invocation).
suggestion: Name the carrier. The plausible ones are: (a) a top-level payload key emitted alongside `skipped_roles` when `prompts` is empty, which the unit is told to obey; (b) the brief command's surrounding text in `next_units[]`; or (c) accept the wasted round-trip and let the hook's stop_hook_active stand-down be the answer, deleting the 'only the instruction' sentence. Whichever is chosen, §6.3 test 9 should assert that the empty-prompt invocation carries the instruction, not just an empty `prompts[]`.

finding: §4.2.3 changes exactly one seam — UnitKind.BriefCommand, which fills next_units[].brief_command — and then rests the interactive-path benefit on it: "the brief is the interactive path's instruction too, where no TP_* variable is set, and a brief that only worked under the driver would leave the operator back at the split script." But the brief a human actually reads from tp resume is a different field: next_action.brief_command (spec/0.35.0.md §9.3), which is phase-level and stays tp review <spec> --round N / tp audit <spec>. tp resume's TTY output prints that field and not the per-unit briefs. Test 15 asserts only next_units[].brief_command. So on the interactive path the operator still receives the whole panel and still needs the split script §4.1 says the flag removes, and the sentence justifying the redundant flag under tp run is buying nothing. Either a second seam has to change or the claim has to be narrowed, and the spec says neither, so the implementer must decide a scope question.
suggestion: State the decision explicitly. Either (a) §4.2.3 also changes the phase-level next_action.brief_command for the review and audit phases, and §6.4 gets a test for it — noting that a phase-level command addresses no single role, so it may have no correct --role value; or (b) say that next_action.brief_command is deliberately unchanged because it names a phase and not a unit, and reword §4.2.3 and §4.3 so the interactive benefit is claimed from next_units[].brief_command, which the operator must read to get it.

finding: §4.2.3 says "The id-to-role mapping is not assumed ... which is why the exit-0 rule exists and why §6.4 test 15 asserts the mapping rather than trusting it." Neither named test can establish it. Test 15 asserts a string — that brief_command interpolates the unit's own id — which is true of any id, correct or not. Test 16 executes each brief and asserts exit 0, but unit ids come from ResolveActiveCorpus, so every id it produces is by construction "recognised" (present in the corpus for the phase); and §4.2.1 makes every recognised name exit 0, with prompts[] possibly empty. So a build in which prompts[].role is not the unit's id — a different derivation, a phase prefix, a display name — passes tests 15 and 16 while every unit under tp run receives zero prompts and does no work. Test 16's own no-checklist-items fixture does not rescue it: exit 0 is the guaranteed outcome there too. The one failure mode §4.2.3 says it is guarding against is the one its guards cannot observe, and as the implementer I have no stated way to know I built the mapping right.
suggestion: Give test 16 a discriminating assertion: for each unit whose role the round emits, the brief's output must carry exactly one prompts[] entry whose role equals the unit's id; only for a unit the round legitimately skips (the no-checklist-items fixture) is prompts: [] the expected result, and the test should assert which case it is per unit rather than asserting exit 0 over both. Then correct §4.2.3's citation to name that test, since test 15 asserts the flag is passed, not that it resolves.

finding: §4.3 books the release's headline payoff as '526,908 emitted bytes down to 49,567 - a 90.6% reduction in bytes handed to units', and that single figure hides two facts that decide whether the flag is earned. Recomputed from §4.1's own round-4 table: of the 477,341 saved bytes, 4 x 82,160 = 328,640 (68.8%) are four copies of the regression prompt - which §4.4 calls a driver defect and Non-Goal 6 declines to fix, and which §4.1 measures as producing zero rows. The remaining 148,701 B is exactly (N-1)/N of the four corpus prompts, i.e. a structural consequence of N units each receiving the panel, not a property of --role: at N=2 it is half as much, at N=5 more. So the release's only benefit number is dominated by an unfixed defect whose repair would remove ~69% of it, and its percentage is a function of this repository's unit count. §4.1 insists that every figure name the round it was measured on precisely because the panel is round-dependent; §4.3's figure names neither its unit count nor its defect share.
suggestion: Split §4.3's figure into its two terms and state both: 'of the 477,341 B, 328,640 B (68.8%) is the regression prompt Non-Goal 6 leaves unfixed, and 148,701 B is (N-1)/N of the corpus panel at N=4'. Then state the residual saving the flag still earns once Non-Goal 6 closes, since that is the number a reader deciding whether --role pays for its surface actually needs.

finding: §6.1 and §7 place mutually exclusive requirements on the same test. §6.1 applies to 'every test below' and closes: 'Any construction that pins those four inputs [round number, loop budget, consecutive-clean count, output_path] satisfies this; one that reads them from the live spec/.tp-review/ tree does not.' Test 14 is one of those tests. §7 then makes test 14 the release's only gate and argues its entire value is that the repository supplies shapes 'occurring for real rather than by construction' — naming 'rounds where regression does and does not emit' as one of them. But regression emission is a function of the round number and of whether findings were resolved fixed (§4.1), i.e. of exactly two of the four inputs §6.1 forbids reading from the live tree. Pinning the round is constructing the shape; reading it is what §6.1 refuses. As written, a conforming test 14 iterates every spec while holding the round constant, which is the fixture §7 says is insufficient, and a test 14 that delivers §7's stated value violates §6.1.
suggestion: Separate the two concerns explicitly. §6.1's four inputs exist to stop a stored fixture encoding one day's state; that goal is met by pinning the inputs to *chosen* values per case, including a round-1 case and a round-N case. Say so, and rewrite §7's justification to rest on what the repository actually varies independently of review state — spec size, section count, corpus presence, heading shapes — rather than on live rounds. Alternatively, exempt test 14 from §6.1's pinning rule and state how it keeps spec/.tp-review/ byte-identical while reading it.

finding: §6.1 offers three isolation mechanisms as interchangeable - 'Whether the isolation is --no-state, a temporary state directory or a copied tree is the implementer's choice; what is fixed is the outcome' - and one of them changes the artifact under test rather than only where state is written. Measured on this spec with the current binary, TP_* cleared: `tp review spec/0.36.0.md` emits 5 prompts with the ax-economist entry at 20,965 B; `tp review spec/0.36.0.md --no-state` emits 4 prompts with that entry at 7,181 B (-66%), reports review_loop.round as 1, and omits `regression` entirely. So an implementer who takes §6.1 at its word satisfies the stated outcome (spec/.tp-review/ and .tp/rounds/ byte-identical) while running §6.3's panel tests against a panel that can never contain the largest entry: test 7's 'a round where regression is emitted' is unreachable, and tests 13, 14 and 17 - the whole-panel equality that §7 makes the release gate precisely because --role's hazard is suppression - pass over a 4-prompt panel. A gate against suppression that can be satisfied by an isolation flag which itself suppresses the biggest prompt is the fixture-flag failure this repository has already been burned by.
suggestion: Delete `--no-state` from §6.1's list of choices, or add the missing outcome to the fixed set: the isolation must leave the emitted panel and every review_loop input identical to a live emission at the round under test, and only redirect where state is written. State it as a property ('the panel the suite tests is the panel a live round emits'), consistent with §6.1's own rule of fixing outcomes rather than harnesses.

finding: §6.1's blockquote is the normative property the tests must establish, and it is arithmetically unsatisfiable as written: "the emitted role prompt equals the same prompt without the clauses plus §2.3's suffix, and differs nowhere else." §2.3's construction is <body, trailing newline removed> + LF LF + clause + LF LF + clause, so the emitted prompt equals the clause-free prompt MINUS one trailing LF plus the 468-byte suffix. §1.1 makes that −1 explicitly load-bearing and not cosmetic. An implementer who implements §6.1's stated equality writes an assertion that fails on every correct build, by exactly one byte. §6.3 test 12 repeats the same omission ("differs from the same tree's pre-clause emission only by the 468-byte suffix"), so the error is in both places a test author would read, and §1.1's own promise that "§6 names whichever applies and never substitutes one for the other" is not kept.
suggestion: Restate the property as: the emitted role prompt equals the clause-free prompt with one trailing LF removed, plus §2.3's 468-byte suffix — a net delta of +467 — and differs nowhere else. Reword test 12 the same way ("differs by removing one trailing LF and appending the 468-byte suffix") so the two figures §1.1 separates are both present in the sentence that uses them.

finding: Test 14 is the release's only gate (§7: 'the gate is §6 test 14 ... Failing it blocks the release'), and it defines its iteration set as 'every spec in spec/ the repository can emit prompts for'. Neither half of that phrase is decidable. Counted in this repository: spec/ holds 38 .md files, of which at least six are not release specs — 0.25.0-role-prompt-research.md, 0.33.0-candidates.md, 0.34.0-candidates.md, 0.34.0-guard-tests.md, 0.34.0-release-counts.md, 0.35.0-candidates.md. tp emits prompts for all 38, so the qualifier 'the repository can emit prompts for' excludes nothing and the unqualified word 'spec' carries the entire filter with no definition anywhere in the document. One engineer iterates spec/*.md (38 files, two phases, 1+N invocations each); another iterates release-numbered files only (26); a third takes the seven CLAUDE.md lists as planned. §7's breadth argument names properties ('specs with deactivated roles, with domain frontmatter, with empty checklists') rather than files, so it cannot settle the choice either. A gate whose subject set is not fixed cannot be reported as passed, and the three readings differ by more than a factor of two in what they cover.
suggestion: State the set as a glob plus an asserted count: 'every file matching spec/*.md — 38 today — run for tp review and for tp audit; the test asserts the number of files it iterated, so a new spec is picked up automatically and a shrunk set fails.' If the non-release notes are meant to be out of scope, give the exact predicate (filename matching ^[0-9]+[.][0-9]+[.][0-9]+[.]md$) and list the excluded files by name, applying §3.1's own rule that a named exclusion beats a silent skip. Also rule on the zero-prompt case: whether a spec that emits no prompts for a phase is a pass, a skip, or a named exclusion.

finding: §1.1's second percentage divides one prompt's delta by the whole panel's bytes. §4.1 establishes the round-4 payload as 131,727 B across five prompts, and §2.3's predicate appends the suffix to every prompt whose output_path is non-empty — all five entries of the default panel, the regression entry included. So the release's delta to that payload is 5 x 467 = 2,335 B, which is 1.77%, not the 0.35% §1.1 states; 0.35% is 467 / 131,727, one prompt's delta over five prompts' bytes. The first figure in the same sentence, 3.77% = 467 / 12,376, is like-for-like and correct, so the pairing reads as one ratio shown at two scales when only one of the two is that ratio. Nothing tests either figure, which is why it can sit here — but the section carrying it opens 'The arithmetic is written out because §6.2 test 5 asserts it as an exact integer' and closes 'Every figure in this spec is stated with the round it was measured on', so it is the section least able to afford an unreproducible number, and a reader deriving the payload cost from it understates the release by a factor of five.
suggestion: Restate the payload figure as the payload's own delta: 'against the whole 131,727-byte payload the same round emits, the release adds 5 x 467 = 2,335 B, 1.77%.' If the intent was instead to show one prompt's delta as a fraction of what a unit receives, label it that way — 'one prompt's 467 bytes are 0.35% of the payload a unit is handed' — so the two numbers are not read as the same quantity measured twice.

finding: §4.2.2 makes the --role refusal 'evaluated **before** the mode's own argument validation', and §6.3 test 10 spends half its construction on making that ordering discriminating (running the refusing modes without their own arguments, then a second partition for --record/--resolve/--resolve-all where it 'cannot be observed'). Nothing on tp's machine-readable surface changes with the ordering: both orders exit 2, and neither exit code nor any JSON key differs. The only thing the rule buys is which flag a human-readable hint names in one mis-invocation. That is a normative constraint on CLI internals, plus a bifurcated test the spec itself admits is unobservable for three of the twelve refusing modes, in exchange for no decision any agent or driver makes differently.
suggestion: Drop the precedence sentence from §4.2.2 and collapse test 10 to the single assertion that matters to a caller: --role with each refusing mode exits 2 and the hint names --role. If the ordering is genuinely wanted, keep it but move it to the acceptance of the task that registers the flag, where its correctness can be established against code - it is the `over-specification` shape, not a contract.

finding: §4.2.2's governing sentence ("--role is legal wherever prompts are emitted and refused with exit 2 where none are") and its table disagree, and the table's two columns do not partition tp review's flag set. Flags that emit prompts and appear in neither column include --no-state, --round, --findings, --final-round and --spec-inline. The rule admits them; an enumeration read as exhaustive refuses them. --no-state is the case that bites: §6.1 proposes it as a test isolation mechanism, so if the table is exhaustive then every test that isolates with it and passes --role exits 2, and the suite cannot be written as specified. As the implementer I must choose between the sentence and the table with nothing to decide on.
suggestion: Say what the table enumerates. If the rows are the mutually exclusive sub-modes, add one sentence — "every other flag rides on the default mode and does not change --role's legality" — and name --no-state, --round, --findings, --final-round and --spec-inline as examples. If the enumeration is meant to be exhaustive over all flags, add the missing ones to the legal column and drop the governing sentence, since it would then be doing no work.

finding: §6.1's first condition asserts an equality over a directory the test suite does not own. 'spec/.tp-review/ and .tp/rounds/ are byte-identical before and after the suite runs, and that equality is itself asserted.' spec/.tp-review/ is written only by tp review/tp audit, so the suite can own it. .tp/rounds/<spec>/<phase>-r<N>/ is the driver's per-unit write target (spec/0.35.0.md §3.3, TP_ROUND_DIR): any role unit running concurrently writes its .ndjson.part there, and this release's own §3.2 clause tells it to write incrementally throughout its run. So the assertion is a claim about the whole machine rather than about the suite, and it fails whenever the suite is run — as tp's project gate requires on every task close — while any review or audit round is in flight. It is also vacuous in a fresh clone and in CI, where .tp/rounds/ does not exist at all, so the assertion passes for a reason unrelated to what it is testing.
suggestion: Scope the assertion to what the suite can own: assert byte-identity of spec/.tp-review/ only, and express the .tp/rounds/ requirement as a negative the suite can actually check — that the suite creates no path under .tp/rounds/ and opens none for writing — or drop it and rely on the isolation mechanism §6.1 already leaves to the implementer.

finding: §6.1's first condition is written as a required assertion — 'spec/.tp-review/ and .tp/rounds/ are byte-identical before and after the suite runs, and that equality is itself asserted' — but no test owns it. §6's tests are numbered 1 through 17 across §6.2, §6.3 and §6.4, and none of them is this one, so it cannot be cited, cannot be reported as passed or failed, and §7 does not gate it. Two further gaps make it unwritable as stated. First, 'byte-identical' is undefined for a directory: file set only, or contents, or mtimes; recursive or top level; and whether a file created and then removed during the suite violates it. Second, .tp/rounds/ is run state rather than review state — no test in §6 invokes tp run except test 15's 'tp run --dry-run', and this spec never says whether dry-run writes there, so the second half of the condition is either an assertion that cannot fail or one whose precondition is undefined. Two engineers write materially different checks and both can claim §6.1 is satisfied.
suggestion: Number it (test 0, or 18) so it has an owner and §7 can cite it, and define the equality operationally: 'the recursive map of relative path to sha256 of file contents under spec/.tp-review/ and under .tp/rounds/ is equal before and after the suite, with a directory that does not exist equal to the empty map.' If .tp/rounds/ is in the condition only because of test 15, state the stronger fact instead — 'tp run --dry-run creates nothing under .tp/rounds/' — which turns a vacuous half into a real assertion about the driver.

finding: Test 4 collects a set and asserts a negative over it without ever asserting the set has members. It 'collects every prompt whose output_path is empty' across five invocations and 'asserts the absence over all of them'. If that collection is empty the assertion holds vacuously — and the collection going empty is exactly the regression the test's own rationale is built on: §6.2 makes the empty output_path the discriminator precisely because the same role name can carry a non-empty one in the default panel. An implementation that assigns a non-empty output_path to the perspective and --verify prompts (the mistake) empties the collection and turns test 4 green while both clauses are appended to every prompt tp emits — the single failure this test exists to catch. The 'derived, not enumerated' argument fixes which MODES are visited and says nothing about whether the derived set is non-empty, so the strengthening §6.2 claims for the derivation does not reach the vacuity.
suggestion: Add the cardinality assertion the derivation needs, before the absence check: 'the collected set contains at least one prompt from each of the five invocations.' Naming the expected count per mode (one each, five in total on today's binary) makes a mode that stops producing an empty-output_path prompt fail loudly rather than silently shrink the test's subject to nothing.

finding: Test 10 excuses three modes from its discriminating case on a premise that is false for one of them: "Where the mode cannot parse without them (--record, --resolve, --resolve-all take a positional) the arguments are supplied and the test asserts the hint names --role, since precedence cannot be observed there." --record does not take a positional — internal/cli/review.go registers it as cmd.Flags().StringVar(&recordPath, "record", "", ...), so it carries its own value and the mode is entered by that value being non-empty. tp review <spec> --role x --record /nonexistent.ndjson therefore enters the record mode with everything else present, and whether the flag-conflict refusal precedes the file check is directly observable — which is the assertion §4.2.2 asks for ("the hint an operator sees names the flag conflict rather than a missing --findings"). Built to spec, the test gives up a discriminating case it could have had, on three modes where only two qualify.
suggestion: Move --record into the discriminating group: run it with a value naming a file that does not exist and assert the hint names the --role conflict rather than the missing file. Keep the weaker carve-out for --resolve and --resolve-all, whose findings NDJSON really is a positional (both are registered as BoolVar), and correct the parenthetical so it names only those two.

finding: Test 11 — '--role with --perspective and with --diff-from exits 0 and emits one prompt' — cannot be written, because --role takes a name and the spec never gives the names three of the four perspectives emit. §4.2 names test-planner for --perspective testing and §4.2.2 names verifier for --verify; no other role name for a perspective appears anywhere in the document. Measured on the freshly built binary against this spec: --perspective documentation emits role documentation-planner, --perspective code-audit emits code-auditor, --perspective regression emits regression. A test author who guesses doc-planner, docs, or audit gets exit 2 under §4.2.1's unknown-name rule, so test 11's outcome turns entirely on a string the spec withholds, and two engineers write tests with opposite results for the same behaviour. §4.2's match-set definition ('what this invocation would emit with --role removed') makes the names derivable at runtime but not writable by a test author reading only the spec, and the same gap reaches test 4, which visits the same four modes.
suggestion: Add the mapping to §4.2.2's table or as a one-line list in §4.2: documentation -> documentation-planner, testing -> test-planner, code-audit -> code-auditor, regression -> regression, --verify -> verifier, stated as measured on the shipped binary. Test 11 can then give the exact invocation per row, and a rename of any of the five fails a test instead of silently changing what --role selects.

finding: Test 9 requires a purpose-built fixture for each of the five skip reasons ('The test builds a fixture per reason rather than asserting the two the driver happens to produce today'), including a domain-mismatch corpus and a --diff-from tree for no-spec-change. By §4.2.1's own rule all five converge on one observable and one branch: the name is present in skipped_roles, so exit 0, prompts: [], reason echoed verbatim - §4.2.1 explicitly declines to give them different treatment ('The hint enumerates the reason, it does not classify the mistake... There is no need to invent a taxonomy'). Five fixtures asserting one contract five times is test surface the contract does not earn, and §4.2.1's table is already the argument for why exit 0 is right.
suggestion: Reduce test 9 to the two reasons that exercise different producers of skipped_roles (one from the unit-dropping filters, one from the prompt-only filters - e.g. disabled-by-spec and no-checklist-items), and assert the shared observable once. If all five are wanted, say what each fixture discriminates that the others do not; otherwise the count is cost without signal.

finding: This round split §4.2 into §4.2.1/§4.2.2/§4.2.3, and five references written against the old single section were not repointed. §4.2 now contains no table at all, yet: test 9 says 'Each of the five skip reasons in §4.2's table' (the skip table is §4.2.1's); test 16 says 'the divergence §4.2's table names' (also §4.2.1's); §7 says 'the five skip reasons of §4.2's table' (same); test 7 says 'This is the rule §4.2 states' (the exit-0/skipped_roles rule is §4.2.1's); test 11 says '--verify is not in this list — it is in test 10's, per §4.2' (the legality table is §4.2.2's). Test 10 gets it right — 'each refusing mode in §4.2.2's table' — which shows the repointing was started and not finished. tp ships a `broken-cross-ref` lint for this class precisely because a reference that resolves to a section without the cited content is the failure mode a reader cannot detect from the citing side.
suggestion: Repoint the five references to §4.2.1 / §4.2.2 as appropriate, and run `tp lint spec/0.36.0.md` before the next round so the class is caught mechanically rather than by a reviewer.
